papers.what_it_is: An early study that casts patch-wise sparse-coding single image super-resolution as a QUBO problem and solves it on a D-Wave Advantage quantum annealer, compared with Lasso, simulated annealing, bicubic interpolation and SwinIR.

existing.note: The paper limits the Lasso statement to compute time (run-time on the cropped Lenna region, Table 2), and the deep learning statement to PSNR accuracy (Table 1). The stored value says far from matching Lasso Regression without naming run-time.
existing.value: The authors state that quantum annealing achieves speed up over classical annealing but is far from matching Lasso Regression's compute time, and that the proposed algorithm is distant from the deep learning-based state-of-the-art image super-resolution result.
quotes: shows that while Quantum Annealing achieves speed up over Classical Annealing, it is far from matching Lasso Regression
While the proposed algorithm is distant from the deep learning-based state-of-the-art image super-resolution result
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
The paper states it in footnote 1 on p.1.

existing.note: The values match Figure 1 and Table 2 (total run-times 658.36 and 89.60). The paper's Table 1 gives the same PSNR values for this cropped region. The run-times compare different hardware (CPU against D-Wave Advantage with server-side overhead), which the paper states on p.5.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that the proposed adiabatic quantum computing algorithm is demonstrated to achieve improved speed-up over a classical analog while maintaining comparable single image super-resolution accuracy.
quotes: The proposed AQC-based algorithm is demonstrated to achieve improved speed-up over a classical analog while maintaining comparable SISR accuracy
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the classical analog is the simulated-annealing variant, not Lasso Regression.
assertions.reader_inference: The speed-up is over classical simulated annealing only. Lasso Regression ran in 4.89 s against 89.60 s for quantum annealing on the one cropped region timed.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to solve the sparse coding problem as a QUBO, the sparse coefficient vector is set to a binary mask m times a fixed vector with all elements equal to a hyperparameter mu, which gives an approximate non-negative l1 optimization problem.
quotes: to solve the problem with QUBO, α is set to be (m µ1), where m is optimized while µ1 is a ﬁxed vector with all elements set to a hyperparameter µ > 0.
This leads to an approximate non-negative l1 optimization problem
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own formulation in Section 4.1 (Eq. 3 and 4).

assertions.value: The authors state that three algorithms, based on the same basic formulation, are tested, and that they differ only by the optimization algorithm used for sparse approximation: Lasso Regression, Classical Annealing and Quantum Annealing.
quotes: With all algorithms being based on the same basic formulation, they differ by the optimization algorithm used for sparse approximation.
Concretely, the optimization algorithms used are (i) Lasso Regression, (ii) Classical Annealing and (iii) Quantum Annealing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section 4.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that Classical Annealing solves the QUBO problem on CPUs with a simulated annealing algorithm from the qubovert library, and that Lasso Regression uses the scikit-learn Lasso solver.
quotes: the scikit-learn Python machine learning library’s linear model.Lasso solver is used
the QUBO problem solved conventionally using CPUs via a simulated annealing algorithm from the qubovert library implemented in C
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own baselines in Section 4.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that Quantum Annealing seeds each patch with a multistart tabu search, selects 32 variables per patch with a heuristic EnergyImpactDecomposer, and so gives each patch a QUBO subproblem of size 32 that is placed along the diagonal of a Q matrix of size 512 by 512.
quotes: The selected variables, numbering 32, are kept track of by index.
each patch is associated with a QUBO subproblem of size 32 and subproblems are added along diagonals of overall Q matrices of size 512
sparse Q matrices of size 512 × 512 that are suitable for the sparse QPU topologies
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own algorithm design in Section 4.2 and Figure 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that Quantum Annealing returns reads from the D-Wave solver, that the high-resolution patch is the weighted mean over the unique solutions with weights set by energy and occurrence, and that these weights define a patch entropy that serves as a metric for uncertainty quantification.
quotes: The HR xi is generated by taking the weighted mean over the unique solutions in Zi.
the patch entropy Hi = − j pij log(pij) can be deﬁned, providing a metric for uncertainty quantiﬁcation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the weighting and the entropy in Section 4.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that dictionaries Dl and Dh are trained with the procedure and the 69-image dataset of Yang et al., and that only 128 atoms are learned in order to accommodate the sparse topology of quantum annealers.
quotes: to accommodate the sparse topology of quantum annealers, a relatively small number of atoms N i.e., 128, are learned by Dl and Dh
a dataset consisting of 69 images used by Yang et al.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own training setup in Section 5.1.

assertions.value: The authors state the hyperparameters: lambda = 10−5 for Lasso Regression, lambda = 0.1 and mu = 0.05 for both annealing algorithms, and Nreads = 100 samples from the annealing solver in Quantum Annealing.
quotes: For Lasso Regression, λ = 10−5 is used.
The annealing-based algorithms share a common set of sparse coding hyperparameters with λ = 0.1 and µ = 0.05.
In Quantum Annealing, Nreads = 100 is used as the number of samples obtained
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own hyperparameters in Section 5.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that evaluation uses three test cases: a 45 × 60 cropped region of the Lenna image with a 15 × 20 downsampled LR version, the full Lenna image, and the Set5 image set, and that the cropped region is the basis of the run-time analysis.
quotes: The ﬁrst test case uses a 45 × 60 cropped region from the Lenna image as the HR ground-truth, with the corresponding downsampled 15 × 20 region as the LR image
The ﬁrst test case of the Lenna image region serves as the basis of a run-time analysis comparing the sparse coding algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own test data and scope in Section 5.1.
assertions.reader_inference: The run-time conclusions rest on one 45 × 60 pixel region.

assertions.value: The authors state that classical algorithms ran on Intel Core 4.00GHz CPUs with 4 cores and 32GB RAM, that Quantum Annealing used the D-Wave Advantage 6.1 QPU with 5760 qubits, that the accuracy metric is the Y-channel PSNR, and that all algorithms upsample by a factor of 3.
quotes: Classical algorithms and client-side data processing are carried out on Intel Core 4.00GHz CPUs with 4 cores and 32GB RAM
uses the D-Wave Advantage 6.1 QPU with 5760 qubits
The accuracy metric used in this work is the Y-channel PSNR
carry out upsampling by a factor of 3.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own hardware and metric in Section 5.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because of the varying nature of the algorithms, the evaluations are carried out on different hardware.
quotes: Due to the varying nature of the algorithms developed, evaluations are naturally carried out on different hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its comparison in Section 5.1.
assertions.reader_inference: The run-time comparison between the classical and quantum variants therefore mixes CPU time with remote QPU service time.

assertions.value: The authors state that the numerical experiments use synthetic Gaussian datasets, each a 756 by 100 data matrix, split into training and validation sets of sizes 36 and 720, simulating sparse coding of a 36 by 100 dictionary with an optimal sparsity of 10 atoms, with results over 20 datasets.
quotes: each dataset is of the form of a data matrix Xall ∈ R756×100 with all elements sampled from the standard Gaussian distribution
with sizes 36 and 720 respectively.
The resulting setup simulates the sparse coding of a R36×100 dictionary with an optimal sparsity of 10 atoms
on 20 datasets generated from a common random process.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own synthetic setup in Section 5.2.

assertions.value: The authors report that Classical Annealing and Quantum Annealing have very similar numerical behavior on the synthetic data, with validation errors around 0.5 at the known optimal sparsity of 10 and the mean validation error of either lying well within the 1σ region of the other.
quotes: Fig.(3b) shows that Classical Annealing and Quantum Annealing have very similar numerical behavior
the validation errors are at around 0.5.
At around α 0 = 10, the mean validation error of either annealing-based algorithm lies well within the 1σ region of the other
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on synthetic data.

assertions.value: The authors report that Lasso Regression achieves better prediction results than the annealing-based algorithms at low sparsities, and that towards the optimal sparsity of 10 its validation error converges to theirs.
quotes: while Lasso Regression achieves better prediction results at low sparsities, towards the optimal sparsity α 0 = 10, the validation error converges to those of the annealing-based algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on synthetic data.

assertions.value: The authors report Y-channel PSNR in dB at magnification factor 3 on the cropped Lenna region, the full Lenna image and Set5: bicubic 28.31, 30.62, 29.35; Lasso Regression 30.22, 31.58, 30.44; Classical Annealing 30.20, 31.70, 30.61; Quantum Annealing 30.19, 31.70, 30.61; SwinIR 31.42, 33.29, 33.89.
quotes: The magniﬁcation factor is 3.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; one run per method as far as the paper states.
assertions.reader_inference: The columns map to the rows in the table's order: Bicubic, Lasso Regression, Classical Annealing, Quantum Annealing, SwinIR. On the cropped region Lasso (30.22) is 0.03 dB above Quantum Annealing (30.19); the paper reports no repeated runs or variance for the image results.

assertions.value: The authors report that Quantum Annealing and Classical Annealing achieve the same PSNR for the two larger test cases at a precision of 2 decimal places.
quotes: the two algorithms achieve the same PSNR metrics for the larger test cases at a precision of 2 decimal places.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the predictive performance of the annealing-based algorithms at the very least matches that of Lasso Regression, and that the results on the larger test cases suggest the possibility of superior performance of annealing-based sparse coding on real images.
quotes: the predictive performance of annealing-based algorithms at the very least matches that of Lasso Regression
suggest the possibility of superior performance of annealing-based sparse coding over conventional sparse coding when the data is in the form of real images
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the authors word it as a possibility.
assertions.reader_inference: On the cropped region the table shows Lasso 30.22 above Classical 30.20 and Quantum 30.19, so at the very least matches holds for the two larger cases only (31.58 against 31.70; 30.44 against 30.61).

assertions.value: The authors state that the sparse coding approaches have accuracies that fall short of the current state-of-the-art SwinIR deep learning model.
quotes: Nevertheless, the sparse coding approaches have accuracies that fall short of the current state-of-the-art SwinIR DL model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: SwinIR is 1.2 dB above the best sparse coding PSNR on the cropped region (31.42 against 30.22) and 3.28 dB above on Set5 (33.89 against 30.61).

assertions.value: The authors report total run-times on the cropped Lenna region of 4.89 s for Lasso Regression, 658.36 s for Classical Annealing and 89.60 s for Quantum Annealing.
quotes: Total Run-time (s) 4.89 658.36 89.60
Run-time results of the algorithms evaluated on a cropped region of the Lenna image
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, one image region.

assertions.value: The authors report that the 89.60 s Quantum Annealing run-time on the cropped Lenna region splits into 31.68 s for CreateQUBO, 55.42 s for AQC preparation, 1.58 s for QPU optimization and 0.92 s for miscellaneous.
quotes: CreateQUBO (s) 31.68 AQC Prep. (s) 55.42 QPU Opt. (s) 1.58 Misc. (s) 0.09 0.12 0.92
Total Run-time (s) 4.89 658.36 89.60
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, one image region.
assertions.reader_inference: The QPU time itself is 1.58 s, about 1.8 percent of the total; the rest is client-side CreateQUBO and server-side communication overhead.

assertions.value: The authors state that the AQC Preparation run-time could not be reduced without fundamental changes to the client-server framework, and that with local QPU access the client-server overhead could in principle be eliminated, making QPU optimization the most significant constituent.
quotes: The AQC Preparation run-time on the other hand, could not be reduced without fundamental changes to the client-server framework on which this work is based.
should local QPU access be possible, the client-server communication overhead could in principle be eliminated
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' claim, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that replacing the tabu search with random initialization and applying quantum annealing over all subsets of m would drastically simplify CreateQUBO but would evidently require more quantum computing resources in terms of access time.
quotes: one possible approach is to replace the tabu search in Algorithm 4 with a random initialization and omit the use of EnergyImpactDecomposer
would evidently require more quantum computing
resources in terms of access time.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' proposal, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the repeated sampling of the D-Wave solver gives Quantum Annealing the advantage of a rapid means for robust prediction and uncertainty estimation compared to classical algorithms.
quotes: This property provides Quantum Annealing with the advantage of providing a rapid means for robust prediction and uncertainty estimation compared to classical algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' claim; the next paragraph says the evidence is insufficient.

assertions.value: The authors state that, due to limited quantum computing resources, insufficient evidence is observed for the advantage offered by robust prediction from the limited evaluations, and leave further numerical experiments and more extensive image evaluations to future work.
quotes: due to limited quantum computing resources, insufﬁcient evidence is observed for the advantage offered by such robust prediction from the limited evaluations.
further relevant numerical experiments and more extensive image evaluations may be the subject of future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit in Section 5.4.

quotes: The vertically oriented stripes in Fig.(6) are due to the column-major nature of the patch-wise iteration in Algorithm 3
where neighboring patches along a column are processed in the same QUBO problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single qualitative demonstration from one study.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that this work has provided some evidence for superior sparse coding performance of annealing-based methods over conventional sparse coding, as an initial demonstration of carrying out SISR with quantum hardware.
quotes: this work has provided some evidence for superior sparse coding performance of annealing-based methods over conventional sparse coding

assertions.value: The paper defines the QAOA ansatz as a Trotterised variational schedule of a cost layer followed by a mixer layer, repeated up to circuit depth L, acting on the initial state with all partitions of the vertex set in equal superposition.

assertions.value: The paper states that the authors simulate the QAOA measurement procedure classically, by computing the probability of measuring the target state in the computational basis, and that the objective minimised by the classical computer is the expectation of the cost Hamiltonian.

assertions.reader_inference: The results are for classically computed probabilities. The paper reports no noisy simulation and no run on quantum hardware; its remarks on noise (higher L raising decoherence impact) are not tested.

assertions.value: The paper states, citing earlier work, that QAOA conforms to the adiabatic theorem: as L tends to infinity the final evolved state converges exactly to the ground state of the cost Hamiltonian and gives the optimal probability, and that such an implementation is unfeasible in the NISQ regime.
quotes: It has been shown that QAOA conforms to the adiabatic theorem, i.e. for L → ∞ the final evolved state |Ψ(θ)⟩ converges exactly to the ground state of HˆC
In practice, such an implementation is unfeasible in the NISQ regime

assertions.value: The authors state that, up to now, the experimental realizations that make use of variational algorithms in the sensing field are still limited to the single-parameter regime.

assertions.value: The authors state that, since the FIM is derived directly from the measured data, all the experimental imperfections are automatically incorporated into the optimization procedure, which thus becomes inherently resilient to noise, and that at no step is knowledge of the sensor response function required.
quotes: Since the FIM is derived directly from the measured data, all the experimental imperfections will automatically be incorporated into the optimization procedure that thus become inherently resilient to noise.
we do not require, at any step of the optimization procedure, the knowledge of the sensor response function, which can remain unknown to its users.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim, tested only in the noise experiments reported later.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the variational approach is resilient to noise and can effectively explore and optimize high-dimensional multi-parameter spaces, making it a promising tool for practical applications in quantum sensing and quantum information processing with photonic circuits, and that the method can benefit quantum photonic protocols requiring gradient evaluation.
quotes: The variational approach is resilient to noise and can effectively explore and optimize the high-dimensional multi-parameter spaces, making it a promising tool for practical applications in quantum sensing and quantum information processing with photonic circuits.
Such a method can benefit in general quantum photonic protocols requiring gradient evaluation.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion; the experiments estimate three phases on one four-mode device.
assertions.reader_inference: The tested problem has three parameters; high-dimensional scaling is not tested.

assertions.value: The paper states, citing earlier work, that variational quantum algorithms are emerging as a promising solution to achieve quantum advantage on the currently available NISQ devices.
